Double Exponential & Approach 1, Approach 2 & \(y = a e^{b x} + c e^{d x}\) & Sum of two exponential terms. It can represent profiles with two apparent rates, but the added flexibility may require more data to estimate stably. \\
Double Exponential (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = w e^{b x} + (1-w)e^{d x}\) & Two exponential components with coefficients w and 1-w, fixing the response at time zero to 1. Examples include fraction remaining or retained properties with two apparent rates. The coefficient and both rates remain fitted; selecting this model does not normalize data. \\
Exponential & Approach 1, Approach 2 & \(y = a e^{b x}\) & Two-parameter exponential relationship. It can describe monotonic change that accelerates or decelerates exponentially over the fitted range. \\
Exponential (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = e^{b x}\) & Exponential profile with amplitude fixed at 1 for responses already on a relative scale, such as fraction remaining or retained mechanical properties. Only the rate parameter is fitted; selecting this model does not normalize data. \\
Exponential + Logistic & Approach 2 & \(y = y_0 - B(1-e^{-k_b x}) - D/(1+e^{-(x-t_{50})/s})\) & Two-phase response profile combining an early exponential change and a delayed logistic transition, with fitted baseline and magnitudes. Examples include multistage changes in mass remaining, molecular weight, or retained mechanical properties. \\
Exponential + Logistic (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = 1 - B(1-e^{-k_b x}) - D/(1+e^{-(x-t_{50})/s})\) & Exponential-plus-logistic response profile with baseline fixed at 1. Both change magnitudes remain fitted, so the terminal response is not fixed. Examples include fraction remaining or normalized retained properties with early and delayed changes. Selecting this model does not normalize data. \\
Finite-Time Power Decay & Approach 2 & \(y = A + (y_0-A) \max(1-kx,0)^n\) & Response profile that reaches zero in finite time, with fitted amplitude, rate, and shape exponent. This surface-erosion form can also be used empirically for remaining mass, volume, molecular weight, or retained mechanical properties when the shape is appropriate. \\
Finite-Time Power Decay (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = \max(1-kx,0)^n\) & Finite-time power-decay profile with amplitude fixed at 1. This surface-erosion form can describe fraction remaining or normalized retained properties when the shape is appropriate. The rate and shape exponent remain fitted; selecting this model does not normalize data. \\
Linear & Approach 1 & \(y = a + b x\) & Straight-line empirical relationship with an intercept and slope. It is appropriate when the in vitro/in vivo relationship is approximately linear over the fitted range. \\
Linear (zero intercept) & Approach 1 & \(y = a x\) & Straight-line empirical relationship constrained to pass through zero. It may be useful when a zero in vitro value should correspond to a zero in vivo value under the selected preprocessing and response scale. \\
Linear + Power Decay & Approach 2 & \(y = y_0 \max\{1-kx-(x/t_f)^n,0\}\) & Empirical remaining-response model combining linear and power-law loss, with the initial response fitted and negative remaining values set to zero. For n > 1, the power term can describe accelerating loss. Requires nonnegative time; k >= 0, tf > 0, n > 0, and y0 >= 0. \\
Linear + Power Decay (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = \max\{1-kx-(x/t_f)^n,0\}\) & Linear-plus-power remaining-response model for data already on a 0-1 scale. The initial response is fixed at 1, leaving the linear rate, power-term time scale, and exponent to be fitted. Requires nonnegative time; k >= 0, tf > 0, and n > 0. \\
Logistic & Approach 2 & \(y = y_0 - A/(1 + e^{-(x-t_{50})/s})\) & Scaled and shifted logistic (sigmoid) response profile with fitted baseline and change magnitude. Examples include delayed changes in mass remaining, molecular weight, or retained mechanical properties. \\
Logistic (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = 1 - 1/(1 + e^{-(x-t_{50})/s})\) & Logistic (sigmoid) response profile with baseline and total change fixed at 1, giving asymptotes at 0 and 1. Examples include fraction remaining or normalized retained properties with a delayed transition. The analyzed response must already match this scale; selecting the model does not normalize data. \\
Logistic + Logistic & Approach 2 & \(y = A\left[w\frac{L(x;k_1,t_1)}{L(0;k_1,t_1)}+(1-w)\frac{L(x;k_2,t_2)}{L(0;k_2,t_2)}\right], L(x;k,t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{k(x-t)}}\) & Weighted sum of two decreasing logistic transitions, with the initial response A fitted and the terminal response fixed at zero. The weight w is the first component's share of the initial response; t1 and t2 locate the transitions, and positive k1 and k2 control their steepness. Requires A >= 0 and 0 <= w <= 1. Examples include two-stage changes in mass remaining or retained mechanical properties. The components are empirical and need not represent physical phases. \\
Logistic + Logistic (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = w\frac{L(x;k_1,t_1)}{L(0;k_1,t_1)}+(1-w)\frac{L(x;k_2,t_2)}{L(0;k_2,t_2)}, L(x;k,t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{k(x-t)}}\) & Weighted sum of two decreasing logistic transitions with the initial response fixed at 1 and the terminal response fixed at zero. The weight w is the first component's initial contribution; t1 and t2 locate the transitions, and positive k1 and k2 control their steepness. Requires 0 <= w <= 1. Examples include fraction remaining or normalized retained properties with two transitions. The components are empirical and need not represent physical phases. Selecting this model does not normalize the input data. \\
Modified Gompertz & Approach 2 & \(y = y_0 - A \exp\{-\exp[(e r_{max}/A)(t_{lag}-x)+1]\}\) & Modified Gompertz response profile with an asymmetric sigmoidal transition, fitted baseline, change magnitude, rate, and lag. Examples include mass remaining, molecular weight, or retained properties with a delayed asymmetric change. \\
Modified Gompertz (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = 1 - \exp\{-\exp[e r_{max}(t_{lag}-x)+1]\}\) & Modified Gompertz response profile with baseline and total change fixed at 1, giving asymptotes at 0 and 1. Examples include fraction remaining or normalized retained properties with a delayed asymmetric transition. Selecting this model does not normalize data. \\
Power & Approach 1 & \(y = a x^{b}\) & Power-law empirical relationship. It can describe nonlinear monotonic relationships where the response changes as a fitted power of time or the mapped predictor. \\
Stretched Exponential & Approach 2 & \(y = a e^{b x^{c}}\) & Exponential relationship with a fitted stretching exponent. It can describe non-single-rate behavior, but the additional shape parameter can increase sensitivity when data are sparse. \\
Stretched Exponential (Normalized) & Approach 2 & \(y = e^{b x^{c}}\) & Stretched exponential profile with amplitude fixed at 1 for responses already on a relative scale, such as fraction remaining or normalized molecular weight. The rate and stretching exponent remain fitted; selecting this model does not normalize data. \\
